items.title: Bench and pedestal grinders
items.text: Before mounting a wheel, inspect it and ring-test it: tap it gently with a light non-metal tool. A dull, dead sound means it may be cracked: do not use it. Check that the wheel's rated speed is at least the grinder's spindle speed. Keep the work rest within 1/8 inch of the wheel and the tongue guard within 1/4 inch, and adjust them as the wheel wears. Wear eye protection with side shields and a face shield if your site requires one.

items.title: Bloodborne pathogens
items.text: Treat all blood and certain body fluids as if they are infectious. If you help someone who is bleeding, put on gloves first if you can, and report any contact with blood. Employers with workers who have occupational exposure need a written exposure control plan. The hepatitis B vaccine must be offered within 10 working days of starting the assignment, after training, unless the worker is already vaccinated or immune.

items.title: Chemical labels and safety data sheets (HazCom)
items.text: Before you use a chemical, read its label and know where its safety data sheet (SDS) is. Every container of hazardous chemicals in the workplace must be labeled. SDSs must be readily accessible to you during every shift in your work area: electronic access is fine if nothing gets in the way. You must be trained on the chemicals in your area when first assigned and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced. If a container has no label, do not use it. Report it.

items.title: Compressed air for cleaning
items.text: Never blow dust or chips off your skin or clothing with compressed air: it can force air or debris into your body. OSHA allows compressed air for cleaning only when it is reduced to less than 30 psi, and only with effective chip guarding and PPE.

items.title: Danger and caution signs and tags
items.text: Obey every sign and tag, and never remove one that is not yours. Danger signs mean an immediate hazard and use red. Caution signs warn of a possible hazard or unsafe practice and use a yellow background with black letters. For accident prevention tags, OSHA recommends red for DANGER, yellow for CAUTION and orange for WARNING.

items.title: Electrical panels: keep the space clear
items.text: Never store anything in front of an electrical panel. For equipment up to 150 volts to ground, OSHA requires clear working space at least 3 feet deep in front, at least 30 inches wide or the width of the equipment, whichever is more, with room for the door to open at least 90 degrees. That working space may not be used for storage, and it must be lit.
items.tags: electrical panel, breaker panel, clearance, 36 inches, 3 feet, storage, blocked panel, panel electrico

items.title: Emergency action plan
items.text: Know your site's alarm, your exit route and your meeting point before you need them. OSHA requires an emergency action plan that covers how to report a fire or other emergency, how to evacuate and which exit routes to use, what employees who stay to run critical operations do before they leave, how everyone is accounted for after evacuating, what employees with rescue or medical duties do, and who to ask about the plan. It must be written and available to employees. A workplace with 10 or fewer employees may share it by word of mouth.
items.tags: emergency, evacuation, evacuate, alarm, muster, meeting point, plan, tornado, earthquake, emergencia, evacuar

items.title: Exit doors and exit routes
items.text: If an exit is locked, chained or blocked, report it to your supervisor now and do not work around it. Exit route doors must open from the inside at all times without keys, tools or special knowledge. Exit routes must be kept free and unobstructed: nothing may be stored in them, even for a short time. An exit route may not pass through a room that can be locked, like a bathroom.
items.tags: exit, door, locked, chained, blocked, egress, fire exit, route, obstructed, salida, puerta

items.title: Extension cords and flexible cords
items.text: Do not use an extension cord with damaged insulation, a missing ground pin or a bad splice. Take it out of service. Unless a specific exception applies, flexible cords may not be used as a substitute for permanent wiring, run through holes in walls, ceilings or floors, run through doorways or windows, attached to building surfaces, or hidden behind walls or ceilings. Cords must have strain relief so a pull does not reach the terminals.
items.tags: extension cord, flexible cord, power strip, daisy chain, splice, permanent wiring, extension electrica

items.title: Eye and face protection
items.text: Wear eye or face protection when there is a hazard from flying particles, molten metal, liquid chemicals, acids or caustics, chemical gases or vapors, or harmful light like welding. Where things can fly, your eye protection must have side protection: clip-on or slide-on side shields that meet the rule are fine. If you wear prescription glasses, you need protection that covers them or has your prescription built in.
items.tags: safety glasses, goggles, face shield, eye protection, side shields, welding, gafas, lentes de seguridad, careta

items.title: Fall protection training
items.text: You must be trained by a qualified person before you are exposed to a fall hazard where you use personal fall protection. Training covers how to recognize the fall hazards in your area, how to reduce them, and how to put on, inspect, use, anchor and store your fall protection the way the manufacturer says. If you have not been trained on the harness or lanyard you were handed, do not use it yet. Ask for training.
items.tags: fall training, harness, lanyard, anchor, tie off, competent, qualified person, arnes, entrenamiento

items.title: Fall protection: the 4-foot rule
items.text: If you could fall 4 feet or more to a lower level from an unprotected side or edge, you must be protected by a guardrail, safety net or personal fall protection system. The same 4-foot rule covers holes, including skylights: they need a cover, guardrail or fall protection. Do not step past a missing guardrail or an uncovered hole. Stop and tell your supervisor. Other heights apply in special cases, like dockboards and fixed ladders.
items.tags: fall, fall protection, 4 feet, edge, hole, skylight, mezzanine, platform, harness, guardrail, caida, proteccion contra caidas

items.title: Fire prevention plan
items.text: OSHA requires a fire prevention plan that lists the major fire hazards and how to handle and store those materials, the ignition sources and how to control them, and the fire equipment for each hazard. It also covers controlling flammable and combustible waste, maintaining safeguards on heat-producing equipment, and who is responsible for ignition and fuel hazards. It must be written and available to employees. A workplace with 10 or fewer employees may share it by word of mouth. Keep flammable scrap and trash from piling up in your area.
items.tags: fire prevention, fire hazard, housekeeping, ignition, combustible, plan, prevencion de incendios

items.title: First aid and eyewash
items.text: If a chemical gets in someone's eyes or on their skin, get them to the eyewash or drench shower right away and call for help. Where eyes or body could be exposed to corrosive materials, OSHA requires facilities for quick drenching or flushing within the work area for immediate use. If there is no clinic or hospital in near proximity, someone on site must be trained in first aid, and first aid supplies must be readily available. Know where your eyewash is before you open a chemical.

items.title: Fixed ladders over 24 feet
items.text: Fixed ladders that extend more than 24 feet above a lower level need fall protection. Ladders installed on or after November 19, 2018 need a personal fall arrest system or ladder safety system. Older ladders may still use a cage or well for now, but by November 18, 2036 all such fixed ladders must have a personal fall arrest or ladder safety system. Use the system that is installed every time.

items.title: Flammable liquid storage cabinets
items.text: Keep flammable liquids closed and in their approved cabinet when you are not using them. A single flammable storage cabinet may hold no more than 60 gallons of Category 1, 2 or 3 flammable liquids, or 120 gallons of Category 4. Keep ignition sources away from where they are used and stored.

items.title: Floors, spills and housekeeping
items.text: Clean up or guard a spill before anyone walks through it, and report hazards you cannot fix. OSHA requires work areas, passageways and storerooms to be clean, orderly and sanitary, floors kept as dry as feasible, and walking surfaces free of sharp or sticking-out objects, loose boards, corrosion, leaks, spills, snow and ice. A hazard must be fixed before anyone uses that surface again, or guarded until it is fixed.
items.tags: housekeeping, spill, slip, trip, wet floor, ice, walking surface, clutter, piso mojado, resbalon, derrame

items.title: Forklift: check it before every shift
items.text: Inspect your forklift before you put it in service, at least once a day. If it is used around the clock, check it after each shift. If anything affects safety, such as brakes, steering, horn, forks, chains, hydraulic leaks, tires or lights, do not drive it. Tag it out and report it. It stays out of service until it is repaired.
items.tags: forklift, powered industrial truck, pre-shift, daily inspection, checklist, montacargas, inspeccion

items.title: Forklift: leaving it parked
items.text: When you leave a forklift unattended, lower the forks fully, put the controls in neutral, shut off the power and set the brakes. Block the wheels if it is on an incline. It counts as unattended when you are 25 feet or more away, or whenever you cannot see it. Even when you are within 25 feet and can see it, lower the forks, neutralize the controls and set the brakes. Keep a safe distance from the edge of docks and ramps.
items.tags: park forklift, unattended, forks down, brake, 25 feet, dock edge, estacionar montacargas

items.title: Forklift: training and evaluation
items.text: Only trained and evaluated operators may drive a forklift. Training covers that type of truck and your workplace, and ends with an evaluation of your driving. Your performance must be re-evaluated at least once every three years. You get refresher training after unsafe driving, an accident or near miss, a poor evaluation, a different type of truck, or workplace changes that affect safe operation.
items.tags: forklift training, certification, license, operator, evaluation, three years, refresher, montacargas, capacitacion

items.title: Gloves, and when not to wear them
items.text: Around rotating parts, such as drill presses, lathes, spindles, rollers and shafts, a glove can be caught and pull your hand in. Follow your site's procedure for that machine. It often means no gloves, no rings, no loose sleeves and hair tied back while the part is turning. Everywhere else, OSHA requires hand protection where hands face cuts, punctures, abrasions, chemical or thermal burns, skin absorption of harmful substances or temperature extremes, and the glove must be chosen for that task.

items.title: Guardrails
items.text: Never lean on, sit on or climb a guardrail, and report one that is loose or damaged. OSHA requires the top rail to be 42 inches high, plus or minus 3 inches, and to hold at least 200 pounds pushed down or out near the top. Openings in the guardrail system may be no more than 19 inches wide.

items.title: Ladders: safe use
items.text: Check the ladder before you use it each shift. If it is damaged, tag it "Dangerous: Do Not Use" and take it out of service. When you climb, face the ladder, keep at least one hand on it, and do not carry anything that could throw you off balance. Use a ladder only for what it was designed for. A portable ladder used to reach an upper level must extend at least 3 feet above that landing. Do not tie ladders together to make them longer unless they are designed for it.

items.title: Lockout/tagout: the steps
items.text: Never put any part of your body into a machine until it is locked out and you have proven it is dead. OSHA sets this order, and your site's written procedure for that machine gives the details: 1. Preparation: know the type and amount of energy, its hazards and how to control it. 2. Shut the machine down the normal way. 3. Isolate it: operate every energy isolating device. 4. Apply your lock or tag to each energy isolating device. 5. Relieve, disconnect, restrain or otherwise make safe all stored energy, such as springs, pressure, hydraulics or capacitors. 6. Verify isolation before you start work, for example by trying the normal start controls, then returning them to off.
items.tags: lockout, tagout, loto, lock out, energy, isolate, verify, try out, zero energy, bloqueo, candado, etiquetado

items.title: Lockout/tagout: whose lock comes off
items.text: Each lock or tag must be removed by the person who put it on. If that person is not available, the employer may remove it only by following a specific procedure: verify the person is not at the facility, make every reasonable effort to reach them, and make sure they know before they come back to work. Never remove someone else's lock. Before locks come off and energy is restored, check that tools and other nonessential items are removed, the machine is intact, and every employee is safely positioned or clear. After the locks come off and before the machine starts, tell the affected employees. The employer must inspect each energy control procedure at least once a year.
items.tags: remove lock, coworker lock, someone else's lock, restart, annual inspection, quitar candado

items.title: Machine guarding
items.text: Run a machine only with its guards in place. If a guard is missing, loose or bypassed, stop and report it. OSHA requires guarding to protect the operator and others from the point of operation (where the work is done), in-running nip points, rotating parts, and flying chips and sparks. Guards must be attached to the machine where possible and must not create a hazard themselves. Machines designed to stay in one place must be anchored so they cannot walk or move.

items.title: Noise and hearing protection
items.text: If you have to raise your voice to be heard an arm's length away, ask whether the area has been checked for noise. Your employer must run a hearing conservation program when exposure reaches an 8-hour average of 85 decibels. That includes monitoring, hearing protection, training, a baseline hearing test within 6 months of first exposure, and a new test every year. The legal limit for 8 hours is 90 decibels, and the allowed time drops as noise goes up: for example 4 hours at 95, 2 hours at 100.

items.title: OSHA rules in OTIS: what they cover
items.text: OTIS summarizes federal OSHA General Industry rules (29 CFR 1910) and injury recordkeeping rules (29 CFR 1904) in plain words, checked against the official text as of November 2026. Nevada and many other states run their own OSHA plan, which can be stricter. A summary is not legal advice: for the exact wording, look up the section number at ecfr.gov or ask your safety lead.

items.title: Overhead cranes: inspections
items.text: OSHA sets two levels of crane inspection: frequent, at daily to monthly intervals, and periodic, at 1 to 12 month intervals. Operating mechanisms and air or hydraulic systems are checked daily, and hooks get a daily visual check plus a monthly inspection with a signed, dated record. Your site's crane program sets the exact schedule. Report any defect before you lift, and never ride the hook or the load.

items.title: PPE training
items.text: Before you work with required PPE, you must be trained on when it is needed, which PPE, how to put it on, take it off, adjust and wear it, its limits, and how to care for it. You must show you understand before doing the work. You must be retrained when the work or the PPE changes, or when it is clear you did not understand. Ask if no one has shown you.

items.title: PPE: hazard assessment and who pays
items.text: Your employer must assess the workplace for hazards that call for PPE, choose the right PPE, and document the assessment in a written certification. PPE required by OSHA is provided at no cost to employees, with some exceptions, such as ordinary steel-toe boots and ordinary prescription safety glasses that can be worn off the job. Damaged or defective PPE must not be used: swap it out before you start.

items.title: Permit-required confined spaces
items.text: Never go into a tank, pit, vault, silo or similar space marked "Danger: Permit-Required Confined Space, Do Not Enter" unless you are an authorized entrant on a signed entry permit. If someone collapses inside, do not go in after them. Call for the trained rescue team and 911. Before entry, the air is tested first for oxygen, then for flammable gases and vapors, then for toxic gases. Oxygen below 19.5 percent or above 23.5 percent is a hazardous atmosphere. An attendant stays outside, watching the entrants, the whole time.

items.title: Portable fire extinguishers
items.text: If your site's plan is to evacuate, pull the alarm and get out: do not fight the fire. Use an extinguisher only if your site has trained you and expects you to, the fire is small, and your way out is clear behind you. OSHA requires portable extinguishers to be visually inspected monthly and to get an annual maintenance check. Employers who expect employees to use extinguishers must train them when hired and at least once a year after that.

items.title: Respirable crystalline silica
items.text: Cutting, grinding or crushing stone, concrete, brick or sand can release silica dust that scars the lungs. Use the dust controls your site provides, like water, vacuum or ventilation, and do not dry-sweep or blow the dust. In general industry, the exposure limit is 50 micrograms per cubic meter as an 8-hour average, and employers must assess exposure at or above the 25 microgram action level.

items.title: Respirators
items.text: Do not use a tight-fitting respirator until you have had a medical evaluation and a fit test for that exact make, model and size. OSHA requires a written respiratory protection program, medical evaluations, fit testing before first use, whenever you change to a different facepiece, and at least once a year after that, plus training, all at no cost to you. A beard or anything that gets between the seal and your face can stop a tight-fitting respirator from sealing.

items.title: Storing oxygen and fuel gas cylinders
items.text: Inside buildings, store oxygen cylinders at least 20 feet from fuel-gas cylinders, like acetylene or propane, and from combustible materials, especially oil or grease. Store cylinders in a well-protected, ventilated, dry place away from heat sources, at least 20 feet from highly combustible materials.
